sections.title: Join Algorithms — When the Planner Picks What

blocks.md: The optimizer is a cost calculator with an uncertain view of your data. Performance work is teaching it: better statistics, better index options, better habits.

Every join carries two competing costs. Startup cost is what it takes before the first row is emitted — building a hash table, sorting an input. Total/per-tuple cost is what each extra row adds over the whole job. Hash join pays setup once (build the hash), then probes every outer row cheaply — the win when both inputs are large and the hash table fits in work_mem. Nested loop pays almost no setup but rescans the inner side for every outer row, so it is only cheap when the outer input is small and the inner is an index probe. Merge join demands sorted inputs, so the query pays a sort (or an already-sorted index scan) up front; it wins on equality-heavy joins where the ordering exists, or where you want sorted output anyway. 'How the planner joins' is really 'which algorithm minimizes estimated total cost for inputs of this estimated size' — and those sizes come from statistics, so stale stats change the join verdict. Read the shape of a plan with EXPLAIN (costs off); the node order and the presence of Hash/Sort nodes tell you more than the numbers.

blocks.md: **Hash Join:** Build side (5000 rows) → hash table in memory. Probe side (10000 rows) → hash probe. If hash table > work_mem → spills to disk (slow). The planner chooses the build side from row estimates — underestimated statistics mean an unexpectedly large hash and a surprise spill. Increase work_mem for big joins.

items.q: A hash join outgrows its memory budget and starts writing hash batches to disk when…
options: working memory (work_mem) is exhausted by the hash table
the table is bigger than 1 GB
no index exists on the join key
items.explain: work_mem controls hash table memory. Spill = massive slowdown. Increase work_mem or reduce the hashed input.

items.q: A merge join demands two sorted inputs. The planner is most likely to pick it when…
options: both inputs already arrive in join-key order, e.g. via index scans
a hash table would exceed work_mem
the WHERE clause filters on one table only
items.explain: Merge Join requires sorted input. Index scan or explicit sort provides ordering.

blocks.md: Planner uses: histogram (most common values), n_distinct, null_frac, correlation. For range: histogram bounds + linear interpolation. For equality: MCV list + 1/n_distinct for non-MCV. For correlated columns: independence assumption (wrong) unless extended stats exist. These numbers ARE the cost model — they pick join order, join method, and index-vs-seq-scan. Stale statistics → wrong cardinality → wrong plan.

blocks.title: Bitmap Index Scan — Multiple Indexes Combined

blocks.md: **Bitmap Index Scan:** Combines multiple indexes in memory (bitmap), then single heap fetch. Great for AND/OR combinations where no composite index exists. Recheck Cond means heap tuple rechecked (lossy pages).

items.q: The planner combines two separate single-column index scans (bitmap AND) mainly when…
options: the query's predicates each match a different individual index
a single composite index already exists
items.explain: BitmapAnd/BitmapOr combines multiple index scans in memory before heap access.

items.q: A Bitmap Heap Scan step that carries a Recheck Cond appears because…
options: the bitmap was stored at page granularity (lossy) so each tuple must be re-verified
the predicate was pushed to storage
items.explain: Lossy bitmap pages store page-level not tuple-level. Must recheck each tuple.

blocks.text: Partial Indexes — Index Only What You Query

blocks.label: partial index
blocks.pg:
-- Partial index (PostgreSQL native)
CREATE INDEX idx ON t (col) WHERE status = 'active';
blocks.mysql:
-- MySQL: no native partial index
-- Workaround: partitioned table or generated column
blocks.py-pandas:
# Filter first, then operate
active = employees[employees['status'] == 'active']
# Then operate on smaller DataFrame

blocks.label: expression indexes & collation
blocks.py-pandas:
# Pre-compute expressions
df['full_name'] = df['first_name'] + ' ' + df['last_name']
events['year_month'] = events['created_at'].dt.to_period('M')

blocks.md: **Expression must be IMMUTABLE.** No NOW(), random(), volatile functions. Expression index stores computed value — if function isn't immutable, index becomes inconsistent.

items.q: A partial index declared WHERE status = 'active' only accelerates queries whose predicates…
options: also pin status to the same constant, e.g. status = 'active' AND salary > 50000
items.explain: Partial index only contains 'active' rows. Predicate must include status='active' to match.
Expression must match exactly. Index on (salary * 12) helps WHERE salary * 12 > 600000.

items.title: Hash vs Nested-Loop Decision
items.statement: Query joins large_table (1M rows) with small_table (100 rows) on id. Which algorithm should the planner pick, and why — in cost terms? What gets built, how many times is the other side read, and what changes if work_mem is tiny?
hints: Hash Join: build a hash on the 100-row side, probe once per large row — ~1M probes, no rescan
Nested Loop would rescan the inner for every outer row, so the 100-row side must be inner
If the hash table exceeds work_mem it spills to disk — re-order inputs or raise work_mem

items.title: Composite Index for Multi-Column Query
items.statement: Query: WHERE user_id = 123 AND created_at > '2024-01-01'. Design index.
hints: Column order: equality first (user_id), then range (created_at)

items.title: Partial Index for Soft Delete
items.statement: 99% queries filter deleted=false. Create partial index on orders(user_id, created_at).

items.title: Covering Index to Avoid Heap Fetch
items.statement: Query: SELECT name, email FROM users WHERE status='active'. Create covering index.

items.title: Fix Non-Sargable: YEAR(created_at) = 2024
items.statement: WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2024 never uses the index on created_at: the function call hides the column from the planner's cost model. Rewrite it as a sargable range so the planner can actually estimate and use the index.
hints: An index on created_at becomes eligible for Index Scan / Bitmap scan once the column stands alone

items.title: Bitmap AND Reasoning
items.statement: Query: WHERE dept_id = 1 AND salary > 50000. There is no composite index, only single-column idx_emp_dept and idx_emp_salary. Justify why the planner combines both via BitmapAnd instead of committing to one index, and when you'd replace them with a composite index.
hints: Each index yields a bitmap; BitmapAnd intersects them in memory; the heap is fetched once
Recheck Cond appears when bitmaps are lossy (page-level, not tuple-level)
When both predicates are highly selective — or the query is hot — a composite (dept_id, salary) index wins

items.title: work_mem Hash Spill Predicament
items.statement: A hash join with a ~2GB build side is orders of magnitude slower than expected. Read the EXPLAIN ANALYZE (it shows hash batches > 1, i.e., spill), then choose mitigations: what does raising work_mem do, and what query-level change could shrink the build side?
hints: EXPLAIN ANALYZE reports 'Hash Batches: 2' or more — the hash table exceeded work_mem and spilled to temp files
Raise work_mem (per-operation memory) so the hash stays resident, or pre-filter rows so a smaller input feeds the hash
The build side is chosen from row estimates — stale stats pick the wrong (bigger) build side

revisionCard: Hash vs Nested-Loop: hash when both inputs are large but the hash fits in work_mem; nested loop when one side is small and the other is an indexed probe
Inner side: nested loop re-probes the inner for every outer row — put the smaller / cheapest input on the inside
work_mem: budget for sorts, hash tables, materialization; exceed it and the hash spills to disk (slow)
Covering index (INCLUDE): index-only scan holds the answer, no heap fetch
Stats freshness: ANALYZE keeps n_distinct, MCV lists, histograms current — stale stats → wrong cardinality → wrong join order
Merge join needs sorted inputs; the sort or an actually-sorted index must beat the hash+nested-loop alternatives

glossary.def: Planner's estimate of work (startup + per-tuple cost) for each plan node; drives join order and node choice.
Build a hash table on one input, probe with the other. Memory-heavy; spills to disk if over work_mem.
For each outer row, probe the inner input. Best when the outer is small and the inner is an index probe.
Both inputs sorted on the join key, then merged linearly. Requires sorted inputs or a sort.
Per-operation memory budget for sorts, hash tables, and materialization. Exceeding it spills to disk.
When an operation exceeds work_mem and writes intermediate data to temp files — much slower than in-memory.
Row-count predictions that statistics feed the planner; selectivity drives the cost model.
Index whose key + INCLUDE payload holds every column a query needs — enabling index-only scans.
